title: Optimal Meeting Point: Fair Ground for Everyone
description: Find the geographic balance point for a group with the Optimal Meeting Point calculator — the fair centre of everyone's locations, on the sphere. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, the balance point of New York, Chicago and Los Angeles sits in Missouri at 40.413, −93.959 — 344 miles from Chicago, 1,045 from New York and 1,401 from Los Angeles.
quick_answer: The Optimal Meeting Point calculator finds the geographic balance point of a set of locations — the spherical centre that treats every traveller's position symmetrically. Enter the group's places and read the central point — the starting answer for meetups and offsites where the venue must be argued fairly.

examples.label: Example · Three cities, one point in Missouri

body.t: New York, Chicago and Los Angeles balance at 40.413, −93.959. Distances from it: Chicago 344 mi, New York 1,045 mi, Los Angeles 1,401 mi — nobody's home turf, which is the point of the exercise.

examples.label: Example · Balance is not the same as least total travel

body.t: Those three cities' total travel from the Missouri centre is about 2,791 miles. Meeting in Chicago instead totals about 2,453 miles — less overall, because Chicago already sits central. The centre optimises fairness of position; the sum is a different optimisation, and the honest planner names which one they chose.

faq: As the spherical mean of the locations — their 3-D vectors averaged and projected back to the surface. It is the same centre the postal-centroid and coordinate-mean tools compute, dressed for meetings.
Does it minimise total travel distance?

Not exactly — the balance (centroid) point and the least-total-distance point (geometric median) differ. With one traveller already central, the median can sit on their city; the centroid stays neutral. This page computes the balance point and says so.
What about road travel instead of straight lines?
Roads bend everything: run the centre, shortlist real towns near it, then compare driving distances for the finalists before deciding.
Duplicate their location to weight it — transparent weighting, visible in the input list rather than hidden in a setting.
The point is in a lake or field.
Balance points are geography, not venues. Treat the point as the centre of the search area and pick the nearest sensible town — the map makes that a two-minute job.
The geometry is global; the practical answer must still respect visas, flight networks and time zones — the centre is the start of the conversation, not its end.
